response:
Consider two primitive polynomials f(x) and g(x) in a UFD R[x]. We want to show that their product f(x)g(x) is also primitive.

Let p(x) be the least common multiple of the denominators of the coefficients of f(x) and g(x). Then p(x) is a unit in R[x], since R[x] is a UFD.

Now, let d(x) be the greatest common divisor of the coefficients of f(x) and g(x). Then d(x) divides both f(x) and g(x), and since p(x) is a unit, d(x) divides f(x)g(x).

On the other hand, since f(x) and g(x) are primitive, their greatest common divisor is 1. Therefore, d(x) = 1, and f(x)g(x) has no common factors with 1.

Hence, f(x)g(x) is primitive.

Now, suppose f(x) and g(x) are coprime in R[x]. We want to show that they are coprime in F[x], the field of fractions.

Let p(x) be the least common multiple of the denominators of the coefficients of f(x) and g(x). Then p(x) is a unit in R[x], since R[x] is a UFD.

Since f(x) and g(x) are coprime in R[x], their greatest common divisor is 1. Therefore, the greatest common divisor of the coefficients of f(x) and g(x) is also 1.

Now, let q(x) be the least common multiple of the denominators of the coefficients of f(x) and g(x). Then q(x) is a unit in F[x], since F[x] is a UFD.

Since the greatest common divisor of the coefficients of f(x) and g(x) is 1, q(x) divides both f(x) and g(x). Therefore, f(x) and g(x) have no common factors with q(x).

Hence, f(x) and g(x) are coprime in F[x].
